question: What training objective does CLIP use to align images and text?
failure_type: Grounded BLIP answer did not satisfy the named CLIP task.
answer: Based on the retrieved evidence (which is about BLIP, not the original CLIP paper), the related training objective described is an image-text contrastive (ITC) loss, which is trained to align the vision and language representations. Evidence: "Unimodal encoder is trained with an image-text contrastive (ITC) loss to align the vision and language representations." This is the contrastive alignment objective. However, the retrieved evidence comes from the BLIP paper (2201.12086v2), not the original CLIP paper, so it describes BLIP's ITC loss rather than explicitly documenting CLIP's own training objective.

arguments.query: CLIP training objective align images and text contrastive

evidence.text: Figure 2. Pre-training model architecture and objectives of BLIP (same parameters have the same color). We propose multimodal mixture

of encoder-decoder, a uniﬁed vision-language model which can operate in one of the three functionalities: (1) Unimodal encoder is trained with an image-text contrastive (ITC) loss to align the vision and language representations. (2) Image-grounded text encoder uses additional cross-attention layers to model vision-language interactions, and is trained with a image-text matching (ITM) loss to distinguish between positive and negative image-text pairs. (3) Image-grounded text decoder replaces the bi-directional self-attention layers with causal self-attention layers, and shares the same cross-attention layers and feed forward networks as the encoder. The decoder is trained with a language modeling (LM) loss to generate captions given images.

We employ a visual transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) as our image encoder, which divides an input image into patches and encodes them as a sequence of embeddings, with an additional [CLS] token to represent the global im- age feature. Compared to using pre-trained object detectors for visual feature extraction (Chen et al., 2020), using a ViT is more computation-friendly and has been adopted by the more recent methods (Li et al., 2021a; Kim et al., 2021).
